scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether calling the police on my daughter for stealing money was the right thing to do. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My daughter is in sixth grade, and every morning I give her a couple of dollars for lunch money. Recently, I noticed that more money was missing than usual. So, I decided to plant a $20 bill to catch her if she took it. She did, and I called the police, asking them to come to the school with me to teach her a lesson about stealing. When we got to the school, my daughter was pulled out of class, and she told the officers that there's a bully who's been stealing her lunch money. She also mentioned that she's been buying lunch for a friend who can't afford it. Both the bully and the friend confirmed this. My daughter was silent on the way home, and I told her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get her into trouble. I also said that in the future, she should talk to me or her mother if there are issues at school, and we'd be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife was really upset. She thinks that this action could lead to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She also mentioned that my daughter would have just lied about stealing in the first place, so I don't understand her idea of a solution. My daughter told my wife that she's terrified that the bully will now retaliate and that she might have lost her friend because of the attention brought to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn't want us to intervene. I'm wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. Did I overreact by involving the police? Should I have handled it differently? What are the potential consequences of my actions? How does my daughter feel about this? How does my wife feel? What could I have done instead to address the issue without causing such distress? Maybe I should consider alternative ways to handle the situation. Instead of involving the police, perhaps I could have talked to my daughter about why she was taking the money, listened to her side of the story, and worked together to find a solution. I could have also addressed the bullying issue directly by talking to the school or the bully's parents. By involving the police, I might have made the situation worse, especially since my daughter was already dealing with bullying and helping her friend. I also need to think about the trust between me and my daughter. By setting up a situation where I caught her stealing, I might have broken her trust in me. She might feel that I don't trust her, which could lead to more problems in the future. It's important to maintain open communication and trust, especially during her formative years. Another thing to consider is the emotional impact on my daughter. Being pulled out of class and having the police involved could have caused her significant stress and anxiety. She might feel embarrassed or ashamed, which could affect her self-esteem and behavior at school. It's crucial to handle such situations in a way that supports her emotional well-being. I should also reflect on my wife's reaction. She's clearly upset and feels that this action could lead to long-term issues in our relationship with our daughter. It's important to communicate with her and understand her perspective. Maybe together we can find a better way to address the issue and repair any damage done. In summary, calling the police on my daughter might have been an overreaction. It could have negative consequences on our relationship, her trust in me, and her emotional well-being. Instead, I should have addressed the issue by talking to her, understanding her reasons, and finding a solution together. I should also address the bullying issue separately to ensure her safety and well-being at school.
